messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Product Manager
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan Mehta is a 58-year-old South Asian man who works as a product manager at a mid-sized technology firm in the Pacific Northwest. He has been married for nearly thirty years, and by most external measures his life in America has been a success — a comfortable home, a stable career, adult children who call regularly. Yet for the past several years, and with increasing urgency over recent months, something has been quietly dismantling the life he built.

Rajan was born in a South Asian country that experienced significant political instability during his early adulthood. In his late twenties, while working as a junior civil servant, he was detained by state security forces during a period of civil unrest. What followed was a period of several weeks during which he was held in an undisclosed location, subjected to physical and psychological torture. The details he has shared in session are fragmentary but vivid: the disorientation of being hooded and moved repeatedly, the sounds of guards speaking in overlapping voices whose words he could not parse, the dizziness that came with sleep deprivation and physical stress until he could no longer tell whether he was standing or falling, the wail of vehicles arriving and departing at all hours. He was eventually released without charge and emigrated to the United States within a year. He has rarely spoken of the detention since.

For decades, Rajan managed. He built routines, worked hard, and told himself that what had happened was behind him. But in the years following the pandemic — with its sirens, its ambient social tension, its disruptions to the predictable structure of his days — something shifted. The symptoms that had always been present at a low level began to press forward.

Now, riding the light rail to his downtown office, Rajan will sometimes hear an ambulance and find himself gripping the seat rail, his breath shallow, scanning the car for exits. The sound does not remind him of the detention in any way he can articulate; it simply arrives in his body as danger before his mind has time to intervene. On days when colleagues crowd around a conference table and several conversations overlap into noise he cannot follow, he feels the same vertiginous pull — a sudden lightheadedness that he has come to associate with losing his grip on reality. He has begun declining in-person meetings where possible, citing scheduling conflicts. His manager has noticed. A project that would have required him to lead a large cross-functional workshop was quietly reassigned, and Rajan told himself he was relieved, though he recognized something had been lost.

Outside the office, he has reorganized his movements around avoidance of anything that might produce stress he cannot control. He takes longer routes to avoid the police precinct two blocks from his gym. When an officer in uniform passes him on the street, he crosses to the other side without quite deciding to. He has stopped attending the community events his wife enjoys, offering vague excuses, and she has stopped asking him to come.

At home, he is not at rest. He wakes in the early hours and moves through the house — checking the locks, standing at the window — not because he expects to find anything but because lying still with uncertainty feels unbearable. During the day he monitors himself constantly, pressing fingers to his wrist to check his pulse, cataloguing any dizziness as a possible signal of something wrong. An unexpected hand on his shoulder from a colleague once produced a sharp, audible intake of breath and a half-step backward that he spent the rest of the afternoon trying to explain away.

What troubles Rajan most is not the symptoms themselves but what he has come to believe they mean. He has arrived at the quiet, settled conviction that the detention happened because of something particular to him — some quality of weakness or visibility that drew it to him — and that this quality has not gone away. He has come to feel that people, even those who appear kind, are operating with interests he cannot see. He told his wife recently, in a rare moment of disclosure, that he does not expect things to get better; he said it matter-of-factly, as though reporting a weather forecast.

It was his wife who finally persuaded him to seek help, after finding him standing in the kitchen at three in the morning, checking that the back door was locked for the second time. What Rajan is most afraid of, he said at intake, is that talking about it will confirm what he already suspects — that what was done to him has permanently changed what he is. What he is most hoping for, beneath that fear, is some evidence that he is wrong.
